refuted.claim: with arbitrary nesting and an optional `direction LR` line per block (inherited from the parent otherwise). See `examples/subgraph.mmd`.
refuted.reason:
The rendering evidence is right, but the README text is not wrong. I rendered examples/subgraph.mmd with the release binary: Auth service, User DB and Broker all sit at x≈191, at y=250, 348 and 472, so the `platform` block's `direction LR` does give way to TD. That outcome is exactly what the README's own Direction bullet (lines 282-285) predicts. `C1 --> Store` links a nested member out of the block, which is the "once a member links out ... the block takes the direction round it" case. The CHANGELOG says the same on purpose, at 0.37.0 Fixed: "every subgraph `direction` in the flowchart corpus and quality fixtures is either linked out of (`advanced`, `subgraph`, the dense fixtures)".

The feature itself works. A cut-down version with no member linking out (`GW --> platform`; `subgraph platform` / `direction LR` / `Auth --> Users --> Bus`) lays the members out in a row, all at y=283.

Line 280 is a syntax sentence. It mentions block syntax, nesting and an optional per-block `direction` line, and the example has all three: `subgraph platform [Platform]`, the nested `events` block, and `direction LR`. Line 280 never says the example shows LR taking effect, and the bullet right after it explains why it doesn't here. So nothing on line 280 is false, out of date or contradicted elsewhere in the README. The finding is a suggestion: either the example should be one where the direction holds, or the pointer should carry a note. That is an editorial or example-design choice, not a README error.

The rendering defect is real, but it is an engine bug. The README text is not wrong.

What checks out: running `flowmaid --advance` on the README block verbatim gives the exact SVG the reviewer quotes. The path is `M 121.8 109.0 ... L 198.5 122.3` with an 11px marker (refX 5), so the head spans about x 193-204. The opaque chip `<rect x="153.7" y="113.3" width="64.7" height="18" fill="#ffffff">` is drawn after the path and covers the head. The diamond polygon (left tip 204.0,122.3) is drawn after the chip and clips the end of "off".

Why the README is not at fault:
1. The JSON is valid and every key in it is documented and real. It parses and renders through the CLI flag the README names. Nothing in the advance section promises where a label chip goes. The only README claim that chips stay clear of boxes (line 649) is about architecture-beta, not advance. CHANGELOG makes no such claim for advance either. So no statement is false, misleading or contradicted.
2. The cause is in src/advance.rs. `label_candidates` (line ~4392) uses the polyline midpoint `points[n/2]` when no vertical leg is at least 22px long. `choose_label_pos` (line ~4452) skips the edge's own endpoint nodes when checking for overlap ("endpoints excluded") and never checks the arrowhead.
3. It is not specific to this example. Any labelled cross-lane edge at the default lane gap does it. With the README JSON minus `"shape": "diamond"` (two plain rects), the path is a straight `M 121.8 109.0 L 208.3 109.0`. The chip `<rect x="181.5" ... width="64.7">` sits centred on the target's left border at x 213.8: it covers the whole head, and the target rect, drawn last, covers half the chip. The text-DSL form (`a -->|hand off| b` across two lanes) gives the same SVG byte for byte as the JSON. A same-lane vertical edge renders cleanly: chip y 143-161, head y 165-176.

The proposed README change would hide the bug, not fix a false claim. A bottom-to-bottom U-route for a plain hand-off between neighbouring lanes is a contrived workaround. It does render cleanly: chip x 59.7-124.4, y 141.3-159.3, head visible at the diamond's bottom tip. But a user's first natural labelled cross-lane edge would still draw its chip over its own head and under its target.

This should be filed against the advance label placement, not the README. Two possible engine fixes: keep chips off the head box and off the target node, or widen the lane gap for a labelled cross-lane edge the way the flowchart layout already makes room for labels.

refuted.claim:
# ported edge: enter b through its top
  c --> b:top
refuted.reason:
The geometry in the finding is right, but nothing in the README is wrong. Rendering the block verbatim with `flowmaid --advance-text` gives a->b `M 100.6 128.0 L 100.6 170.5`, a dashed green line with a green marker. It gives c->b `M 237.3 122.3 L 143.2 122.3 L 143.2 158.0 L 100.6 158.0 L 100.6 170.5`, with a grey marker drawn after the green one. So the last 12.5px and the arrowheads do coincide.

Every statement around this example is still accurate:
- The example parses and renders.
- `c --> b:top` really enters b through its top, as the comment says.
- "A ported edge's first/last segments leave the sides perpendicularly" holds.
- The `style a-->b color:#188038,dash:4 2` line still visibly applies: the line is green and dashed from y=128 to y=158.

The Advance section never promises that edges stay apart. The "never drawn onto an unrelated edge" sentence is in the Architecture section and covers only that renderer. The README has no picture of this output, so it shows nothing wrong either.

The overlap is a limit of the engine, not a mistake in the docs. In src/advance.rs around line 4495, `fan_key` only spreads edges that share the same from/to terminal pair. Two edges from different sources into the same side of b both land on its centre point. A port pins that point, so the router has to pay the overlap cost; with an automatic end, `c --> b`, it routes cleanly into b's right side instead. docs/design/advance-terminals-and-router.md:106 says the share cost is meant to stop edges lying on top of each other. The real fix is to spread the terminal points of distinct edges on one side, and that belongs in the engine's tracker.

Changing the README to use an example that avoids the case would hide the engine issue rather than correct a false claim. It is a choice of example, not a documentation error.

refuted.claim: - [x] `subgraph` — nesting, titles, per-block `direction`, edges to/from a subgraph *(v0.5.0, v0.7.0)*
refuted.reason: The version tags are historically correct. Per-block `direction` first shipped in 0.5.0. Commit 475fb79 ("subgraph support (#2): nesting, titles, per-block direction, mermaid claim semantics; 0.5.0") added `Subgraph::direction` and a recursive `layout_frag` in src/scene.rs. That function lays out each subgraph in its own direction: `let dir = level.and_then(|l| g.subgraphs[l].direction).unwrap_or(inherited_dir); ... syn.direction = dir;`. Its examples/subgraph.mmd is titled "Nested subgraphs with a per-block direction". `layout_frag` still exists at v0.16.0. It is gone at v0.17.0, removed by 5aa02d4/02f3a71 ("global subgraph layout"). So the CHANGELOG line "It used to be read only to keep a subgraph's edge-less members on one row" describes 0.17.0 to 0.36.0, not 0.5.0. The finding's main point, that crediting 0.5.0 is wrong, does not hold. CHANGELOG 0.37.0 lists the change under "Fixed", which means a regression was repaired, not a new feature. The roadmap does not re-tag other items when they are later fixed. The checkbox is also true today: rendering `flowchart TB; X --> s; subgraph s; direction LR; A --> B --> C; end` with the release binary puts A, B and C on one row (all at y=166, inside a 310x92 frame). The detailed rule is already documented in the README's Subgraphs section (lines 282-285) and the pipeline overview (line 803). Adding "(v0.37.0)" to the roadmap would be extra information, not a fix for a false or misleading claim.

refuted.claim: (old README.pre-tidy.md:462) "... and so do its members nothing links into — edge-less ones, chains of their own, ones linking onward and ones leading to a member the feeder links to (that member then sits a row lower) — instead of on the drawing's first layer beside the feeder; a node outside that only those members link into moves down with them, and a subgraph they link into follows a row further down, whole."
refuted.reason: The new Layers bullet (README.md:797) is accurate, so this is a terseness complaint, not a real problem. Everything it states checks out against src/layout.rs:2441-2486 (the seat_box_sources doc). A box fed from outside every box goes on the row just below its topmost outside feeder. Its source members (members nothing links into) are ranked no higher than that row. It stays put when it has no feeder outside every box, when a cycle breaker reaches a source from outside, or when seating would move an outside node that does not "hang below the move" ("unless that would stretch another node's edges"). The binary agrees with all of this. For `flowchart TB / hub --> a1 / subgraph g[box] / a1 / loose / end / loose --> out` it gives hub y=47, a1 and loose y=171, out y=269, so the box is seated. Adding `pin --> out` gives loose and pin y=87 (level with the hub), out y=185, so it is not seated because pin's edge would stretch. The dropped details follow from the layering the bullet already describes. A node only those members link into has to sit below them, and a fed member a seated member leads to has to sit a row lower. The "would stretch another node's edges" clause only makes sense if seating can move nodes downstream, so the bullet already implies they move. Nothing in the new text is false, contradicted elsewhere in the README, or likely to mislead a reader about behaviour. Dropping secondary consequences from an overview bullet is the "merely terse" case the review rules exclude.

NARROW_AREA_SLACK is 0.02 (:121), NARROW_LEN_SLACK is 0.1 (:124) and NARROW_FLOW_SLACK is 0.15 (:139). The bullet also leaves out other limits that the old text never named either, such as NARROW_CROSS_SLACK and NARROW_HIT_SLACK. So it was always a summary, not a complete list. Putting the example clause back is a completeness or wording choice, not a fix for a real problem.
